name: Students and research
title: Printing, annotating and citing for coursework and research
metaDescription: Print academic PDFs two-up and duplex, annotate them so the notes survive to June, cite web pages in APA, MLA and Chicago, and stop slides eating a ream.
intro: A reading list is a printing problem before it is a reading problem. Twelve papers at twenty-four pages each is nearly three hundred sheets if you let the printer have its way, and a sixty-slide deck at one slide per page is sixty more. These four guides cover the settings that turn a paper into six sheets instead of twenty-four, the annotation habits that survive until revision week, and the citation formats markers actually check.
answer: Students save the most paper by printing academic PDFs two pages per sheet and double-sided, which turns a 24-page paper into six sheets. Annotate the PDF rather than the paper copy so highlights stay searchable, and record the author, title, date, URL and access date for every web source you cite.
primaryKeyword: how to print and annotate academic papers

posts.title: How to print journal articles and papers properly
posts.metaTitle: How to Print Journal Articles Properly
posts.metaDescription: Print journal articles and papers without burning a ream: two pages per sheet, duplex, binding margins and right settings for JSTOR, PubMed and arXiv PDFs.
posts.answer: Open the PDF in a real reader rather than the journal website, then print two pages per sheet, double-sided, in greyscale. That turns a 24-page paper into six sheets. Add a binding margin if you will punch or staple it, and test on the first four pages before running the rest.

body.x: A twenty-four page paper with two columns, four pages of references and a figure every third sheet will eat a quarter of a ream if you let it. Academic PDFs are actually the easiest documents to print economically, because the publisher already laid them out for paper. You just have to stop your printer treating one PDF page as one sheet.
Print from the PDF, never from the journal website

Publisher article pages on ScienceDirect, Wiley Online Library and SpringerLink are full-screen applications: floating toolbars, a citation widget, a "recommended articles" rail and a figure viewer that loads images only when you scroll. They print badly and routinely split a figure across two sheets.

Almost every one has a **Download PDF** button. Use it. The PDF is typeset at a fixed size, carries the real journal page numbers you need for citations, and prints exactly as the editors intended. If the HTML version is all you have, run it through the [web page printer](/print) first.

Hitting a paywall? Search the exact title on Google Scholar and look for the `[PDF]` link beside the result, which usually points at an author copy in an institutional repository. PubMed Central, arXiv, bioRxiv and SSRN are all free.
Two pages per sheet is the single biggest saving

Academic PDFs are typeset for a page, so the margins are generous and the type is large enough to survive shrinking. Two portrait pages side by side on one landscape sheet scales each to roughly 65 percent, taking 11pt body text to about 7pt, comfortable at desk distance.

body.caption: What 11pt body text becomes at each n-up setting.
head: Pages per sheet
Effective scale
11pt text becomes
Verdict
rows: The sweet spot for single-column papers and preprints

body.x: Two-up fails on dense two-column journals. Elsevier and Springer set body text at roughly 9pt, which at 65 percent becomes 5.8pt in a 45mm column. Print those one page per sheet and save elsewhere, on duplex and greyscale.
Then print on both sides
Two-up plus duplex is a four-fold reduction: twenty-four pages become six sheets.

items.h: Open the file in a proper PDF reader
items.x: Browser PDF viewers hide the settings you need. Use Adobe Acrobat Reader, Preview on macOS or Evince on Linux, and check the page count first.

items.h: Open Print and find the sizing panel
items.x: Press Ctrl+P or Cmd+P. In Acrobat Reader the section is called **Page Sizing & Handling**. On macOS it is the **Layout** pane of the system print sheet.

items.h: Choose Multiple, two pages per sheet
items.x: Click **Multiple**, set **Pages per sheet** to 2 and **Page order** to Horizontal. The orientation flips to landscape by itself. Leave "Print page border" off.

items.h: Turn on double-sided with the right flip
items.x: Tick **Print on both sides of paper**. Because two-up rotates the sheet to landscape, the right choice is **Flip on short edge**, the opposite of the portrait default. Get it backwards and every second sheet reads upside down: [the full rule is here](/blog/save-ink/print-double-sided).

Tick **Print in grayscale (black and white)**, just under the copies field in Acrobat Reader. On an inkjet this stops the printer mixing cyan, magenta and yellow into a composite black, which is what silently drains colour cartridges.
Set the range to `1-4` and print. Check page 2 is on the back of page 1 the right way up, and nothing is clipped at the spine.

body.x: Leave room for the staple or the hole punch
Journal PDFs use symmetric margins, so a three-hole punch lands in the text on one side of every sheet, and a corner staple eats the first line of every page. Three ways round it:

items: **Shrink and shift.** Set **Custom Scale** to 92 percent in Acrobat Reader. The page is redrawn smaller and centred, adding roughly 8mm of white space on every edge, enough for a three-hole punch.
**Staple top-left, print one-sided.** If you will write on the pages anyway, single-sided gives you a clean back for notes.
**Use a wallet instead of a punch.** It keeps the margins intact and survives a rucksack better than staples.

body.x: If a paper matters enough to keep, do not punch the only copy. Paper is for reading; the file is the archive. [Annotate the PDF](/blog/students/annotate-pdf-for-study) instead.
Notes for the main sources

What you get
Best settings
rows: A US Letter PDF with a licence cover page. Older material is a scan with no text layer
Print from page 2. OCR it first to search or highlight

Take the PDF. Two-up works well
A LaTeX-built US Letter PDF, wide margins, often 11 or 12pt single column

One page per sheet, duplex, greyscale. Two-up is too small

One page per sheet. Download the chapter, not the book

body.x: Make one reading pack instead of ten print jobs
Ten separate jobs means ten walks to the printer and ten chances to leave one behind. Build a pack instead:

items: Rename the PDFs `01-author-year.pdf`, `02-author-year.pdf` and so on, so they sort in reading order.
Merge them into a single file with the [PDF merger](/tools/merge-pdf).
[Add page numbers](/blog/watermark/add-page-numbers-to-pdf) so you can say "pack page 41" in a seminar.
Print the whole pack once, two-up and duplex.

body.x: Turn this week’s reading list into one file, in the order you plan to read it.
What it actually costs
A mono laser page costs 2 to 4 cents in toner plus a cent in paper; an inkjet page with colour figures costs 8 to 15 cents. One 24-page paper:

items: One page per sheet, single-sided, colour inkjet: 24 sheets, close to **$2.90**.
One page per sheet, duplex, mono laser: 12 sheets, about **$0.72**.
Two-up and duplex, mono laser: 6 sheets, about **$0.18**.

body.x: Across a thirty-paper reading list that is roughly $87 against roughly $5 a term, and 720 sheets against 180. The settings take thirty seconds once; your reader remembers them.
Reading pack too large to email round the study group? Compress it first.

If the file is a scan with no text layer, run [OCR](/blog/ocr/how-to-ocr-a-scanned-pdf) before printing so your copy stays searchable. Then see [annotating PDFs for studying](/blog/students/annotate-pdf-for-study).

faqs.q: How do I print two pages of a PDF on one sheet?
faqs.a: In Adobe Acrobat Reader, open Print, find Page Sizing & Handling, click Multiple, and set Pages per sheet to 2 with Page order Horizontal. On macOS the same control is in the Layout pane of the print sheet. Browser PDF viewers do not offer it.

faqs.q: Why is my two-up printout too small to read?
faqs.a: Two-up scales each page to about 65 percent, so 11pt text lands near 7pt. That is fine for single-column preprints but not for two-column journals typeset at 9pt, which end up near 5.8pt. Print those one page per sheet instead.

faqs.q: How do I print a JSTOR article without the cover page?
faqs.a: Set the print range to start at page 2. The licence cover is always the first page. If you plan to keep the file, delete that page from the PDF once so every future print job skips it.

faqs.q: What margin do I need for a three-hole punch?
faqs.a: About 12mm of clear space on the punched edge. Since journal PDFs use symmetric margins, set Custom Scale to 92 percent in the print dialog, which adds roughly 8mm on every edge and is enough for standard punches.

faqs.q: Should I print papers at all, or just read them on screen?
faqs.a: Print the ones you will read closely and annotate by hand; read the rest on screen. Printing every paper on a reading list is the most common source of wasted paper in a department, and most of those printouts are skimmed once.

posts.title: How to annotate PDFs for studying
posts.metaTitle: How to Annotate PDFs for Studying
posts.metaDescription: Annotate PDFs so the notes still help in June: a colour system, margin notes in your own words, free apps for Windows, Mac and iPad, and exporting highlights.
posts.primaryKeyword: how to annotate a pdf for studying
secondaryKeywords: best pdf annotation app for students
posts.answer: Read once without marking anything, then highlight on a second pass using a fixed colour code and write a margin note in your own words beside every highlight. Use Zotero or Adobe Acrobat Reader on a laptop, GoodNotes or Notability on an iPad, and export the highlights into your notes before revision starts.

body.x: Most PDF annotation goes wrong in the same way: a first read with the highlighter already in hand, half the page turns yellow, and in June the highlights say nothing that the plain text did not. The fix is not a better app. It is a two-pass habit and a rule about what a highlight means.
Highlighting on its own does almost nothing

When cognitive psychologists ranked common study techniques by how well they hold up in controlled experiments, highlighting and rereading came out near the bottom, while self-testing and spaced practice came out on top. Highlighting is not useless, but it only earns its place when it feeds something else: a question, a flashcard, a paragraph you write yourself.
A highlight is a promise to come back. If you are never coming back, do not make it.

So the working rule is: **every highlight gets a margin note**, and every margin note is in your own words. If you cannot restate the sentence, you have not understood it, and colouring it in will not help.
The two-pass method

items.x: Five to ten minutes. Title, abstract, section headings, figures, conclusion, and a glance at the reference list. You are deciding whether this paper deserves a second pass at all. Roughly half do not.

items.h: Pass two: read and highlight sparingly
items.x: Set yourself a budget: no more than one sentence in ten. If more of the page is coloured than not, you are marking topic rather than argument.
Attach a sticky note or text comment to each highlight while the sentence is still in your head. Aim for one line: "claims X causes Y, sample only 42 undergrads".

At the end of the section, convert two or three notes into questions you could be asked. "Why does the effect disappear above 30 degrees?" A question you can answer later is worth ten highlights you cannot.

items.h: Export before you close the file
items.x: Pull the highlights and notes into a single document per topic, with page numbers. This is the artefact you will revise from. The PDF is the source, not the study material.

body.x: Use a colour code and never change it
Four or five colours, one meaning each, applied identically across every paper for the whole term. The value is in the consistency, not in the specific mapping.

body.caption: A colour system that survives a term. Adapt the meanings, then leave them alone.
head: Colour
Means
What you do with it later
rows: A core claim or a definition
Evidence: a number, an effect size, a sample
Goes in the results table of your notes

body.x: You cannot highlight text that is not there. A scanned PDF is a picture of a page: the highlighter tool will either be greyed out or will draw a free-form box that never matches the line. Run [OCR](/blog/ocr/how-to-ocr-a-scanned-pdf) first to add a real text layer, then annotate.
Scanned chapter or a photographed handout? Add a searchable text layer before you start marking it up.
Which app, on which machine

body.caption: Annotation tools compared on what matters for study: cost and whether the highlights ever leave the file.
head: Platform
App
Cost
Getting the highlights out
rows: None. Highlights save into the file and stay there
Print → **Summarize Comments** produces a printable list of every comment with its page number
View → **Highlights and Notes** opens a sidebar listing every mark; select all and copy
Export the annotated PDF; handwriting stays searchable inside the app
Best in class. Right-click the item → **Add Note from Annotations** turns every highlight into a note with page numbers and a live citation

body.x: If you are managing more than about twenty sources, the Zotero route is worth the afternoon it takes to set up. It stores the PDF, the annotations and the citation metadata in one record, so the highlight you made in February is still attached to the reference you need in May. Everything else on that list is a reader that happens to write marks into a file.
Notes on the iPad workflow

items: An **Apple Pencil** changes the maths. Handwritten margin notes are faster than typing and, in GoodNotes and Notability, still searchable.
Import PDFs into the app rather than annotating in Files, or your marks end up scattered across three places.
Set the app to a **two-page spread** for two-column journal PDFs; single-page view forces constant zooming.
Back up. An annotated PDF that exists only inside one iPad app is one restore away from being gone.

body.x: Before you hand anything in or share it

Annotations are live objects. Anyone who opens your PDF can drag your notes around, delete them, or read the comments you meant only for yourself. If you are sending a marked-up paper to a supervisor or a study group, flatten it first so the marks become part of the page.
Flatten comments and highlights into the page before you send a marked-up PDF to anyone.
Paper still wins for some things

Dense mathematics, anything you need to sketch alongside, and long theory chapters are genuinely easier on paper with a pencil. The sensible split is: annotate digitally the things you will search later, and print the things you will think with. If you are printing, do it economically, see [printing journal articles properly](/blog/students/print-journal-articles) and [printing lecture slides](/blog/students/print-lecture-slides). And when you quote anything you found online, record the details you will need for [the citation](/blog/students/cite-a-web-page) while the tab is still open.

faqs.q: What is the best free PDF annotator for students?
faqs.a: Zotero 7 if you are managing a reference list, because it exports every highlight into a note with page numbers and citations. Adobe Acrobat Reader if you only need to mark up individual files, and Microsoft Edge if you want zero installation on Windows.

faqs.q: Why can I not highlight text in my PDF?
faqs.a: The file is almost certainly a scan with no text layer, so there are no characters to select. Run OCR on it to add one, then the highlighter will snap to lines normally. A locked or permission-protected PDF can also block commenting.

faqs.q: How do I export all the highlights from a PDF?
faqs.a: In Zotero, right-click the item and choose Add Note from Annotations. In Adobe Acrobat Reader, open Print and click Summarize Comments. On macOS Preview, open View → Highlights and Notes and copy the sidebar list. Edge has no export at all.

faqs.q: Do annotations stay in the file if I send it to someone else?
faqs.a: Yes, and they stay editable, so the recipient can move or delete them. Flatten the PDF first if you want the marks to be permanent and non-editable, which is also what you want before submitting anything.

faqs.q: Is it better to annotate on paper or on a tablet?
faqs.a: Paper is better for material you need to think through, sketch alongside or read in one long sitting. A tablet is better for anything you will need to search or quote later, because the highlights stay attached to text you can find again.

posts.title: How to cite a web page in APA, MLA and Chicago
posts.metaTitle: Cite a Web Page: APA, MLA and Chicago
posts.metaDescription: Correct APA 7th, MLA 9th and Chicago 17th formats for citing a web page, with examples, what to do when the author or date is missing, and access date rules.
posts.primaryKeyword: how to cite a web page
secondaryKeywords: citing a website with no author
do i need an access date
posts.answer: Every web page citation needs five things: author, publication date, page title, site name and URL. APA 7th puts the date in brackets after the author, MLA 9th italicises the site name and drops the https prefix, and Chicago 17th offers a footnote and a bibliography form. Add an access date when there is no publication date.

body.x: Every style guide asks for the same five things: **who** wrote it, **when**, **what** it was called, **where** it lives, and **how** to get back to it. Collect those while the tab is still open and the formatting is mechanical. Lose them and you spend an evening reverse-engineering a citation from a half-remembered headline.
Bold below stands in for italics. Punctuation, capitalisation and element order are exactly as the current handbooks specify.
The three styles at a glance

body.caption: Current editions and their headline differences for web sources.
head: Style
Current edition
In-text form
Access date policy
rows: Only when the content is designed to change and is not archived
Optional, and recommended whenever there is no publication date
A numbered footnote, or (Kelly 2026) in author-date
Only when no publication or revision date can be found

body.x: Style guides move. Chicago released an 18th edition in 2024 and departments adopted it at different speeds, so a rubric saying "Chicago" may mean either edition. Check your handbook, and ask before you format 60 references twice.
APA 7th edition
Pattern: Author, A. A. (Year, Month Day). **Title of the page in sentence case**. Site Name. URL
Worked example: Kelly, R. (2026, March 4). **How microplastics enter the food chain**. National Geographic. https://www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/microplastics

items: Page titles are **sentence case**: capitalise the first word and proper nouns only.

When the **author and the site are the same organisation**, give the name once as the author and omit the site name. World Health Organization. (2025, June 12). **Air quality guidelines**. https://www.who.int/…
No date? Use `(n.d.)` in the date position.
APA no longer wants "Retrieved from"; the bare, unshortened URL is correct.
For a direct quote from an unpaginated page, cite a paragraph or heading: (Kelly, 2026, para. 4).

body.x: MLA 9th edition
Pattern: Author Last, First. "Title of the Page." **Title of the Website**, Day Month Year, URL. Accessed Day Month Year.
Worked example: Kelly, Rebecca. "How Microplastics Enter the Food Chain." **National Geographic**, 4 Mar. 2026, www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/microplastics. Accessed 9 Sept. 2026.

items: Page titles are **title case** in quotation marks; the site name is italicised.
MLA 9 **drops the `http://` or `https://`** from the URL. Everything after that stays.
Months are abbreviated except May, June and July: Jan., Feb., Mar., Apr., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov., Dec.
The access date is optional but recommended, and effectively required when there is no publication date.
In-text, an unpaginated web source is cited by author alone: (Kelly). Never write "n. pag."

body.x: Chicago 17th edition
Chicago runs two systems. Humanities courses usually want **notes and bibliography**; social sciences usually want **author-date**.
Notes and bibliography
Footnote: 1. Rebecca Kelly, "How Microplastics Enter the Food Chain," National Geographic, March 4, 2026, https://www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/microplastics.
Bibliography: Kelly, Rebecca. "How Microplastics Enter the Food Chain." National Geographic, March 4, 2026. https://www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/microplastics.
The note uses commas and first-name-first; the bibliography uses full stops and inverts the name. That is the commonest Chicago mistake.
Author-date
Reference list: Kelly, Rebecca. 2026. "How Microplastics Enter the Food Chain." National Geographic. March 4, 2026. https://www.nationalgeographic.com/environment/microplastics.
In-text: (Kelly 2026). No comma between name and year, which is where APA users trip.
Chicago asks for an access date only when you cannot find a publication or revision date, and it goes just before the URL: "accessed September 9, 2026, https://…".
When something is missing

body.caption: Web pages routinely lack an author or a date. Here is what each style expects instead.
head: Missing
APA 7
MLA 9
Chicago 17
rows: Move the page title into the author slot
Begin the entry with the title
Begin with the title, or use the site as author
Describe the page in square brackets
A named person (an organisation wrote it)
Use the organisation; omit a duplicate site name
Name the section or heading in the note

body.x: Why the access date is not busywork

A printed article is fixed. A web page is a moving target: prices change, statistics get corrected, policies are quietly rewritten, pages disappear. The access date is the only element that tells a reader which version you read.

The problem has a name, link rot, and it is worst where you would least hope. A widely cited Harvard study of United States Supreme Court opinions found roughly half the linked sources no longer resolved, and newspaper-archive audits have found a quarter of deep links dead within a few years. A citation with no access date and a dead URL is unverifiable.
Archive the source, not just the link

items.x: Paste the URL into the Wayback Machine at web.archive.org and use **Save Page Now**: a permanent, timestamped, third-party copy anyone can check. For law and policy work, Perma.cc does the same with an institutional guarantee.
Public archives miss paywalled and script-heavy pages. Clean it with the [web page printer](/print) and save a PDF of what you actually read.

items.h: Stamp the retrieval date onto it
items.x: A PDF stamped "Retrieved 9 September 2026" is unambiguous a year later, when the file metadata has been rewritten by three syncs.

items.h: Cite the original, and note the archive
items.x: Give the live URL as normal. If the page has already vanished, cite the archived version and say so, all three styles allow it.
A Zotero record holds the metadata, the snapshot and your annotations together, so citation and evidence never drift apart.

body.x: Turn the page you are citing into a clean, dated PDF you can file alongside the reference.
Stamp the retrieval date across your captured page so the copy speaks for itself.
Let software do the formatting, but check it

Zotero, Mendeley and the citation tools in Word and Google Docs all produce a formatted entry from a URL, and all fail in predictable ways: a section name mistaken for an author, sentence-case titles capitalised, a publication date buried in the metadata missed, and a retrieval date APA no longer wants appended. Generate, then check each entry against the patterns above.

For the mechanics, see [saving a web page as a PDF](/blog/save-pdf/save-webpage-as-pdf-chrome) and [paper versus PDF for records](/blog/print/print-web-page-to-pdf-vs-printer). For marking up sources, see [annotating PDFs for study](/blog/students/annotate-pdf-for-study).

faqs.q: Do I need an access date when citing a website?
faqs.a: In APA 7 only when the content is designed to change and is not archived, such as a live map or a wiki. MLA 9 makes it optional but recommends it. Chicago 17 wants it only when no publication or revision date exists. When in doubt, include it.

faqs.q: How do I cite a web page with no author?
faqs.a: Move the page title into the author position. APA puts the title first followed by the date in brackets; MLA and Chicago simply begin the entry with the title. If an organisation clearly owns the content, use the organisation as the author instead.

faqs.q: Should the URL be a live hyperlink in my bibliography?
faqs.a: APA 7 accepts either plain text or a live link as long as the formatting is consistent through the document. MLA 9 and Chicago 17 both accept plain text. Never use a shortened URL, and never break a URL with a manual hyphen.

faqs.q: What is the difference between APA 6 and APA 7 for websites?
faqs.a: APA 7 drops the "Retrieved from" prefix before URLs, drops retrieval dates for most sources, and adds the site name as a separate element after the title. If your reference begins "Retrieved from http", you are still writing APA 6.

faqs.q: Can I cite a page that has since been deleted?
faqs.a: Yes. Cite the archived capture: give the original details, then the archive URL and the capture date. All three styles accept an archived version, and a Wayback Machine link is far stronger evidence than a dead original.

posts.title: How to print lecture slides without wasting 60 pages
posts.metaTitle: Print Lecture Slides Without Wasting Paper
posts.metaDescription: Print lecture slides as 3, 6 or 9 per page, kill the animation build steps that triple the page count, and turn a 60-slide deck into five duplexed sheets.
secondaryKeywords: print pdf slides multiple per page
print slides in black and white
posts.answer: Use handout mode rather than full-page slides: three per sheet if you want ruled note lines, six per sheet for revision. Delete the duplicate pages that animation build steps create in a PDF export, and print in greyscale so dark slide backgrounds do not drain a cartridge. Sixty slides then fit on five duplexed sheets.

body.x: A sixty-slide deck printed straight from the lecturer’s PDF is sixty sheets, most of them nine-tenths empty, and if the deck used animations it can easily be a hundred and eighty. Two settings fix almost all of it, and neither takes longer than the walk to the printer.
First: why the page count is wrong

When a lecturer exports slides with animations to PDF, most tools write **one page per build step**. A slide that reveals four bullet points becomes four near-identical pages. This is where "sixty slides" turns into a hundred and eighty, and no handout setting will fix it, because as far as your printer is concerned those really are different pages.

items: If the lecturer posted the original **.pptx or .key file** on Moodle or Canvas, use that instead. PowerPoint prints the final state of each slide and never duplicates.
In **Keynote**, untick **Print each stage of builds** in the print sidebar and the duplicates vanish.
If a **LaTeX Beamer** deck is yours to rebuild, `\documentclass[handout]{beamer}` collapses every overlay into one frame.
If a PDF is all you have, delete the duplicate pages once and keep the cleaned file.

body.x: Strip the duplicate build-step pages out of a slide PDF before you print or file it.
Then choose the right handout layout
A 16:9 slide is 338mm wide at full size. Everything below follows from how much of that width survives on an A4 sheet.

body.caption: Based on a 16:9 deck printed on A4 portrait with 12mm margins. "24pt" is typical slide body text.
head: Layout
Slides across
Slide width on A4
24pt slide text prints at
Use it for
rows: Almost never. One sheet per slide
Dense diagrams and charts you must actually read
Live lectures. The only layout with note lines
Text slides you will annotate lightly
Revision. 60 slides become 10 sheets, or 5 duplexed
The cheapest option on the list by a wide margin

body.x: The **3 slides per page** handout is the one people miss. It is the only layout that prints ruled note lines beside each slide, which is exactly what you want in a live lecture. Six per page is for revision, when you already have the notes.

Notice that 4-up and 6-up produce identical slide widths for a 16:9 deck, because both use two columns. Six per sheet is therefore free relative to four: same legibility, a third less paper. There is almost never a reason to choose 4-up.
Where the setting lives

head: App
Where handout mode lives
Killing the build steps
rows: File → Print → the **Full Page Slides** dropdown → Handouts
Not needed. PowerPoint prints each slide once
File → Print preview, then the layout dropdown in the grey toolbar
File → Print → **Grid** or **Handout** in the sidebar
A PDF export of any deck
Acrobat Reader → Print → **Multiple** → Pages per sheet
Delete the duplicate pages from the PDF first
The handout option collapses every overlay

body.x: Kill the colour before it kills a cartridge

Modern slide templates are dark: white text on a near-black background. Printed as-is, every sheet is a solid rectangle of toner, the white text is a hole in it, and the paper comes out damp and curled on an inkjet. A single dark deck can visibly move the ink gauge.

items: In PowerPoint, open the **Color** dropdown in the print pane and choose **Pure Black and White**. This is not greyscale: it converts fills to white and keeps outlines, so dark slides print as normal documents.
In Keynote, tick **Black and white** in the print sidebar.
In Google Slides, open File → Print preview and tick **Hide background** in the grey toolbar. That is the control that strips the dark fill.
If you are stuck with a PDF, choose greyscale in the printer properties and accept a grey page, or ask the lecturer for the source file. There is no reliable invert-for-print in Acrobat Reader.

body.x: Greyscale is not the same as Pure Black and White. Greyscale renders a black background as black; it only stops the printer mixing colour inks. For dark decks you need the black-and-white conversion, which lives in the slide app, not in the printer driver.
The whole workflow, once

items.x: Open the file and look at the last page number. If it is far higher than the number of slides the lecturer talked about, you have build-step duplicates.

items.h: Get the source file if you can
items.x: Look on Moodle or Canvas for a .pptx or .key alongside the PDF. It solves the duplicates, the dark background and the handout layout in one move.
Three per page for a lecture you are about to sit through. Six per page for revision. Outline if you only want the words.
Pure Black and White for dark templates, greyscale for light ones. Do this in the slide app before you reach the printer driver.
Portrait handouts use **Flip on long edge**. Six per sheet duplexed puts twelve slides on one physical piece of paper.
Look at the preview. If slides 40 to 60 are the exam-relevant ones, print `40-60` and leave the rest on screen.

body.x: When you only want the words

For text-heavy decks, Outline mode is the most underrated setting in PowerPoint: it prints the title and bullet text with no slide frames, no images and no background, turning a sixty-slide deck into three or four pages. If all you have is a PDF, extracting the text gives you the same thing, and it drops straight into your notes.
Pull the text out of a slide PDF when you want the content, not the slides.

Once the handout is printed, the rest is study method rather than printing, see [annotating PDFs for studying](/blog/students/annotate-pdf-for-study) for what to do with the note lines. For the settings that apply to every document you print, [fitting more on a page](/blog/save-ink/fit-more-on-a-page) and [saving ink](/blog/save-ink/save-ink-when-printing) cover the rest.

faqs.q: How do I print 6 slides per page in PowerPoint?
faqs.a: File → Print, open the dropdown that says "Full Page Slides", and choose Handouts → 6 Slides Horizontal. Horizontal reads left to right, vertical reads top to bottom; horizontal matches how the deck was presented.

faqs.q: Why does my slide PDF have three times as many pages as slides?
faqs.a: The deck used animations and the export wrote one page per build step. Get the original .pptx or .key file if you can, or delete the duplicate pages from the PDF. No print setting can merge them back.

faqs.q: How do I print slides with the speaker notes?
faqs.a: Choose Notes Pages in the same print dropdown. It prints one slide per sheet with the notes underneath, so it is expensive: only use it when the lecturer actually wrote substantial notes rather than reminders to themselves.

faqs.q: How do I stop dark slides printing as solid black?
faqs.a: In PowerPoint choose Pure Black and White in the Color dropdown, which converts fills to white while keeping outlines and text. Greyscale will not help: it prints the dark background as grey. Keynote has an equivalent Black and white option.

faqs.q: How many slides per page is still readable?
faqs.a: Six per sheet on A4 keeps 24pt slide text at roughly 6.5pt, which is readable at desk distance. Nine per sheet drops it to about 4pt, which is only good for finding a slide, not for reading it.
